questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about delusion is false?

options.text: It is a false belief based usually on incorrect inference about external reality.
It is firmly sustained despite what almost everyone else believes.
It is firmly sustained despite what constitutes as obvious proof or evidence to the contrary.
It is usually not preceded by a delusional mood.
The belief is not accepted by other members of the person’s culture or subculture.

correct_answer.text: It is usually not preceded by a delusional mood.

correct_answers.text: It is usually not preceded by a delusional mood.

questions.explanation: A primary delusion is a delusion that arises full formed without any connection with previous events. It could be preceded by a delusional mood in which the person is aware of something strange and threatening happening.

questions.question_text: A man with a phobia of open spaces is made to draw up a hierarchy of situations, from the least anxiety provoking to the most anxiety provoking. He is then taught relaxation techniques and gradually exposed to the hierarchy of situations that he has previously drawn up. This is known as
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitization is based on the behavioural concept of reciprocal inhibition. This holds that relaxation inhibits anxiety so that the two are considered to be mutually exclusive. During this treatment, patients are successfully exposed (either in reality or in imagination) to stimuli in the hierarchy, beginning with the least anxiety-provoking event and then to the most anxiety-provoking event, with each exposure being paired with relaxation.

questions.question_text: In order to determine whether a client is suitable for intensive psychotherapy, which one of the following needs to be assessed?
questions.explanation: An assessment and analysis of personality and intelligence is essential to determine whether the client is suitable for psychotherapy.

questions.question_text: An electrocardiogram (ECG) tracing was done as part of the annual assessment for a schizophrenia patient who is on follow-up with the outpatient service. The corrected QTC was noted to be 750 ms. Which of the following medications is most likely to be responsible for this?
questions.explanation: The cardiac QT interval is a useful, but imprecise, indicator of risk of torsades de pointes and increased cardiac mortality. Quetiapine has been shown to have a moderate effect on the QTC interval (meaning that it has been observed to prolong the QTC by more than 10 ms on average when given at a normal clinical dose). Clozapine, risperidone and olanzapine have a low effect. Other risk factors for QTC prolongation include: cardiac history, previous long QT syndrome, bradycardia, ischaemic heart disease, myocarditis, myocardial infarction, electrolyte abnormalities and female gender.

questions.question_text: A 22-year-old male has been feeling increasingly troubled by his neighbours, as he believes that they are spying on him consistently. He does not report any other perceptual abnormalities and there has not been any decline in terms of his functioning. The most likely clinical diagnosis would be
questions.explanation: A delusional disorder is largely an ill-defined condition manifesting as either a single delusion or a set of delusions, being persistent and at times lifelong, and not having an identifiable organic basis. There are occasional or transitory auditory hallucinations, particularly in the elderly. Delusions are the most conspicuous or the only symptoms and are present for at least 3 months. For the diagnosis to be made, there must not be any evidence of schizophrenic symptoms or brain disease.

questions.question_text: A core trainee has been asked to obtain collaborative history from the family members of a patient who has just been admitted. According to the family members, the patient has been having behavioural changes for the past 6 months. At times, he would be laughing to himself, and he has shown a general decline in his personal functioning. He does have delusional beliefs and auditory hallucinations. Which subtype of schizophrenia would this be?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis is likely to be hebephrenic schizophrenia. The mean age of onset is usually between 15 and 25 years. It is associated with a poor prognosis. Affective changes are often prominent. Fleeting and fragmentary delusions and hallucinations, disorganised thoughts, rambling speech and mannerisms are common. Negative symptoms such as flattening of affect may also be observed.

questions.question_text: An elderly old man looks into the mirror and is shocked that he is unable to see himself in the mirror. What form of psychopathology is this?
questions.explanation: In autoscopy, the person sees himself or herself and knows that it is him or her. Negative autoscopy occurs when the person looks into the mirror and cannot see one’s own image.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man, John, has just been discharged from the ward following treatment for first-episode psychosis. He is followed up closely by his community psychiatric nurse. She is concerned that when John is at home, he is being subjected to critical and harsh remarks from his father. She is asking the multi-disciplinary team to consider other interventions that might be appropriate for John. Which of these interventions would be the most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Family therapy would be recommended in this case. External indicators for family therapy include John’s recent diagnosis and role change in the family; internal indicators include communication problems and triangulation. Family therapy, by introducing humour, warmth and role-playing, helps modify both verbal and non-verbal communication within the family.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old male has been recently diagnosed with first-episode psychosis. He started on an antipsychotic risperidone around 4 weeks ago. The community psychiatric nurse reports that there has not been any improvement in his symptoms. As a core trainee, what would you want to consider?

options.text: Increasing the dose of the medication

questions.explanation: Patients with first-episode psychosis need at least 6 months of antipsychotic treatment to assess response. A common reason for lack of improvement at 4 weeks is non-concordance. It is important to explore adherence issues before increasing dose or changing medication.

questions.question_text: With regards to the treatment of Wernicke’s encephalopathy, which of the following should be administered first?
questions.explanation: Wernicke’s encephalopathy is a medical emergency. Intravenous thiamine (vitamin B1) should be given first to prevent further neurological damage and progression to Korsakoff’s syndrome.

questions.question_text: Based on the International Classification of Diseases (ICD)-10 and Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)-5 classification system, which of the following psychiatric disorders is believed to be part of a continuum between schizophrenia and mood symptoms?
questions.explanation: Schizoaffective disorder is believed to lie on the continuum between mood disorders and schizophrenia, with both affective and schizophrenic symptoms prominent in the same episode or closely linked episodes.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about persuasion is incorrect?

options.text: Audience identification with the communicator plays a key role in persuasion.
Views of reference groups usually do not play a role if the communicator is credible and has expertise.
High self-esteem and intelligence of the recipient increase the likelihood that complex communications will be persuasive.
Simple message repetition can be a persuasive influence leading to attitude change.
A low anxiety recipient is more influenced by a high fear message and vice versa.

correct_answer.text: Views of reference groups usually do not play a role if the communicator is credible and has expertise.

correct_answers.text: Views of reference groups usually do not play a role if the communicator is credible and has expertise.

questions.explanation: This statement is incorrect. Views of reference groups remain important for persuasion even when the communicator is credible. Repetition, message complexity, self-esteem and anxiety all modulate persuasive impact.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old Malaysian man is referred by police for psychiatric assessment. A few days ago, he was arrested by police for shoplifting in the supermarket. Then, he became mildly depressed because he ‘lost face’ after the incident. This morning, he took a knife and tried to kill pedestrians who walked across his path. He is amnesic for the episode. This man suffers from which of the following culture-bound syndromes?
questions.explanation: Amok (Malay: to ‘run amok’) is a culture-specific syndrome characterized by an explosive homicidal outburst followed by amnesia for the event and sometimes suicidal acts.

questions.question_text: All of the following are considered to be part of the normal stage of grief with the exception of
questions.explanation: The classic stages of normal grief are denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. Agitation may occur but is not a recognized standalone stage.

questions.question_text: A 22-year-old male has been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and sectioned for treatment in the mental health service three times since the onset of his schizophrenia. He has had an adequate trial of haloperidol and olanzapine, which did not help with his symptoms. It is now decided that he start on a trial of clozapine. Which one of the following investigations should be considered before starting him on clozapine?
questions.explanation: Clozapine carries a risk of agranulocytosis. A baseline full blood count is mandatory prior to initiation and at regular intervals thereafter.

questions.question_text: A patient presents with catatonia to the outpatient clinic and a joint decision was made for inpatient admission for further treatment. The trainee should expect to find the following signs of catatonia, with the exception of
questions.explanation: Catatonic signs include ambitendency, automatic obedience, Mitgehen, negativism, echolalia, echopraxia, stereotypy, waxy flexibility and verbigeration. Neologisms are newly coined words and are a thought-disorder feature rather than catatonia.

questions.question_text: A 22-year-old male came for his routine outpatient clinic follow-up and he reported that he had been troubled by voices recently. He shared that he was worried about the voices, as the voices seemed to be commenting on what he is doing. The psychopathology being described would be
questions.explanation: Running commentary is a complex auditory hallucination in which voices comment on the person’s ongoing actions or thoughts, often in the third person.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man suffers from alcohol dependence. His general practitioner (GP) asked him to take disulfiram but no clear instruction was given. Every time he drinks alcohol, he takes disulfiram. He develops flushing of the face, headache, vomiting, chest pain and sweating when he drinks alcohol. He attributes the unpleasant experiences to alcohol and he has decided not to drink alcohol in his life. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: Aversive conditioning uses an unpleasant stimulus (here the disulfiram-alcohol reaction) to reduce or eliminate an undesired behaviour (drinking).

questions.question_text: A 21-year old male has a history of bipolar disorder and he has been previously admitted thrice for manic episodes and just recently for a depressive episode. During his routine outpatient review, the core trainee noted that the patient has pervasively low mood with reduced interest and fulfils the criteria for bipolar, depressive episode. Which of the following medications would be most suitable for him?
questions.explanation: Lamotrigine is effective for bipolar depression and for preventing further depressive episodes, with low risk of mood switching or rapid cycling. Its main side-effect is rash, especially with rapid dose escalation.

questions.question_text: This is a particular subtype of schizophrenia in which there might be marked psychomotor disturbances that might alternate between extremes. In addition, the patient might also report experiencing a dream-like state with vivid scenic hallucination.
questions.explanation: Catatonic schizophrenia may present with psychomotor extremes (stupor or excitement) and is often associated with dream-like states and vivid scenic hallucinations.

questions.question_text: A 75-year-old woman has suffered from a recent cerebrovascular accident (CVA). After the CVA, her family members note that she has global dementia and associated frontal lobe personality changes. Which of the following might be implicated?

options.text: Infarction of the anterior cerebral arteries
Infarction of the middle cerebral arteries
Infarction of the posterior cerebral artery

correct_answer.text: Infarction of the anterior cerebral arteries

correct_answers.text: Infarction of the anterior cerebral arteries

questions.explanation: Anterior cerebral artery infarction can produce frontal lobe signs (personality change, dysexecutive function) and lower-limb weakness with sparing of arms and face.

questions.question_text: A medical student being attached to the addiction specialty wonders how long an individual needs to have symptoms of alcohol dependence in order for a diagnosis to be made. The correct answer, based on the ICD-10 classification system, would be
questions.explanation: The ICD-10 requires the presence of three or more dependence criteria for at least 1 year to diagnose alcohol dependence syndrome.

questions.question_text: There are five types of social powers that have been proposed. Which of the following types of social power best describes someone who is often being looked up to as a role model, is well liked by many and has the ability to make people around them feel good?
questions.explanation: Referent power derives from charisma and the ability to attract others. People comply because they identify with or like the power holder.

questions.question_text: The following defence mechanism is commonly used in borderline personality disorder:
questions.explanation: Splitting—viewing others and self as all good or all bad—is characteristic of borderline personality and serves to manage intolerable ambivalence.

questions.question_text: A patient with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) tends to make use of this particular defence mechanism:
questions.explanation: Reaction formation—adopting attitudes directly opposite to unacceptable impulses—is common in OCD (e.g. extreme cleanliness to counteract unacceptable impulses).

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications would be the most helpful for patients diagnosed with catatonia?
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines (e.g. lorazepam up to 4 mg daily) are first-line for catatonia. Electroconvulsive therapy is an alternative. Underlying causes include schizophrenia, mood disorders, organic conditions and certain drugs.

questions.question_text: A welfare organization decides to hire a man with schizophrenia for vocational training. This man will be paid £400 at the end of each month if he can make 100 key chains per month. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: A fixed-interval schedule delivers reinforcement (payment) after a fixed time period (one month) if the performance criterion (100 key chains) is met.

questions.question_text: The following best describe auditory hallucinations that psychotic patients experience, with the exception of

options.text: Voices telling them that they are useless

correct_answer.text: Voices telling them that they are useless

correct_answers.text: Voices telling them that they are useless

questions.explanation: Voices telling the patient they are useless are mood-congruent content, not true auditory hallucinations of the psychotic type. Auditory hallucinations in psychosis include command voices, derogatory voices, running commentary and voices arguing.

questions.question_text: Which of the following factors account for the lower incidence of alcoholism in Orientals?

options.text: Presence of ultra-rapid metabolizing CYP 450 enzymes

questions.explanation: Many Orientals have an inactive form of aldehyde dehydrogenase, leading to acetaldehyde accumulation and flushing. This aversive reaction protects against alcoholism.

questions.question_text: Which of the following personality disorders might be present in someone who presents with the psychiatric diagnosis of malingering?
questions.explanation: Malingering—intentional feigning of symptoms for external gain—is associated with antisocial personality traits such as deceitfulness, lack of remorse and disregard for others.

questions.question_text: On examination of a patient’s visual field, the examiner would ask the patient to cover one eye and fixate on the examiner’s opposite eye. Mapping of the visual field is then carried out by the examiner. The objective of this examination is to check for

options.text: Checking for presence of organic disorders (myasthenia gravis or thyroid eye disease)
Assessment for lesions involving the central visual pathway

correct_answer.text: Assessment for lesions involving the central visual pathway

correct_answers.text: Assessment for lesions involving the central visual pathway

questions.explanation: Confrontation visual field testing assesses the integrity of the central visual pathways. Lesions at various points produce characteristic field defects (e.g. bitemporal hemianopia, homonymous quadrantanopia).

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old university student presents with delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech and grossly disorganized behaviour for 3 weeks. He failed an examination 3 weeks ago. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: This patient does not fulfill both DSM-IV-TR and ICD-10 diagnostic criteria for brief and acute psychotic disorders respectively.
This patient fulfills the DSM-IV-TR diagnostic criteria for brief psychotic disorder.
This patient fulfills the ICD-10 diagnostic criteria for acute and transient psychotic disorder.
This patient fulfills both DSM-IV-TR and ICD-10 diagnostic criteria for brief and acute psychotic disorders respectively.
DSM-IV-TR diagnostic criteria for brief psychotic disorder do not consider the person’s culture.

correct_answer.text: This patient fulfills the DSM-IV-TR diagnostic criteria for brief psychotic disorder.

correct_answers.text: This patient fulfills the DSM-IV-TR diagnostic criteria for brief psychotic disorder.

questions.explanation: DSM-IV-TR requires brief psychotic disorder to last at least 1 day but less than 1 month. ICD-10 acute and transient psychotic disorder requires onset and resolution within 2 weeks. Cultural factors can be considered in DSM-IV-TR.

questions.question_text: Colon cancer patients have a tendency to compare themselves with other patients who are deemed to be more ill than them. Which of the following terminology best describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Downward social comparison occurs when individuals compare themselves to others who are worse off, which can bolster self-esteem.

questions.question_text: Attitudes are made up of which of the following components?
questions.explanation: Attitudes comprise an enduring organisation of motivational, emotional, perceptual and cognitive processes toward some object or issue.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old female has been too afraid recently to step out of her house. She feels that other people around her can know what she is thinking just by looking at her. This form of psychopathology is known as
questions.explanation: Delusion of reference is the false belief that events, objects or people in one’s environment have special significance or are directly related to oneself.

questions.question_text: A talented child believes that he will get the highest marks in class if he wears a red watch on the day of examination. When he does not have an examination, he usually wears a blue watch. The interval for him to get the highest mark varies. Nevertheless, his habit of wearing a red watch during examination remains stable over the years. He tends to wear the red watch more often if he has not obtained the highest marks in class for a long time. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: A variable interval schedule provides reinforcement (highest marks) after unpredictable time intervals, producing a moderate, steady response rate that is relatively resistant to extinction.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man suffering from schizophrenia used to take chlorpromazine 100 mg orally per day. He wants to change antipsychotics and requests a list of drugs. Which of the following lists indicate the correct dosage which is equivalent to oral chlorpromazine 100 mg per day?

options.text: 0.5 mg/day haloperidol; 0.5 mg/day risperidone; 2.5 mg/day olanzapine; 37.5 mg/day quetiapine; 15 mg/day ziprasidone; 3.75 mg/day aripiprazole
1 mg/day haloperidol; 1 mg/day risperidone; 2.5 mg/day olanzapine; 37.5 mg/day quetiapine; 30 mg/day ziprasidone; 3.75 mg/day aripiprazole
1.5 mg/day haloperidol; 1.5 mg/day risperidone; 2.5 mg/day olanzapine; 37.5 mg/day quetiapine; 30 mg/day ziprasidone; 3.75 mg/day aripiprazole
2 mg/day haloperidol; 2 mg/day risperidone; 5 mg/day olanzapine; 75 mg/day quetiapine; 60 mg/day ziprasidone; 7.5 mg/day aripiprazole
4 mg/day haloperidol; 4 mg/day risperidone; 10 mg/day olanzapine; 150 mg/day quetiapine; 120 mg/day ziprasidone; 15 mg/day aripiprazole

correct_answer.text: 2 mg/day haloperidol; 2 mg/day risperidone; 5 mg/day olanzapine; 75 mg/day quetiapine; 60 mg/day ziprasidone; 7.5 mg/day aripiprazole

correct_answers.text: 2 mg/day haloperidol; 2 mg/day risperidone; 5 mg/day olanzapine; 75 mg/day quetiapine; 60 mg/day ziprasidone; 7.5 mg/day aripiprazole

questions.explanation: Oral chlorpromazine 100 mg is approximately equivalent to haloperidol 2 mg, risperidone 2 mg, olanzapine 5 mg, quetiapine 75 mg, ziprasidone 60 mg and aripiprazole 7.5 mg daily.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is considered to be a poor prognostic factor for patients with schizophrenia?

options.text: No ventricular enlargement on computed tomography (CT) imaging

questions.explanation: Male gender is a poor prognostic factor. Good premorbid social adjustment, family history of affective disorder, short duration before treatment, paranoid subtype, affective symptoms and good initial response predict better outcomes.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old male sustained head injuries, after being involved in a major road traffic accident about one year ago. Recently, his wife has noticed marked changes in his behaviour. She is concerned especially about him making inappropriate, rude sexual remarks when he is out. The symptoms that he is currently experiencing suggest an injury to which part of his brain?
questions.explanation: Frontal lobe injury leads to personality changes (disinhibition, inappropriate remarks), poor judgment, perseveration and executive dysfunction.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman develops brief psychosis following childbirth. In order for her to fulfil the diagnostic criteria for postpartum psychosis, which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.text: The DSM-IV-TR specifies the onset of her psychotic episode has to be within 4 weeks postpartum.
The ICD-10 states that her psychotic episode should commence within 6 weeks of delivery.
The DSM-IV-TR provides postpartum onset specifier associated with brief psychotic disorder.
In the ICD-10, her condition is classified under schizophrenia.
There is no specific diagnostic criterion for postpartum psychosis in the DSM-IV-TR and the ICD-10.

correct_answer.text: In the ICD-10, her condition is classified under schizophrenia.

correct_answers.text: In the ICD-10, her condition is classified under schizophrenia.

questions.explanation: In ICD-10 postpartum psychosis is coded under F53 (mental and behavioural disorders associated with the puerperium), not under schizophrenia (F20). DSM-IV-TR includes a postpartum onset specifier for brief psychotic disorder.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old specialist registrar was at the annual Royal College of Psychiatrists academic conference. There were a lot of participants and she was having a discussion with Professor Brown regarding her latest research. She was able to identify Professor Wilson, who called out for her. Which form of attention process was she using?
questions.explanation: Selective/focused attention (the 'cocktail party effect') allows one to attend to a single stimulus (Professor Wilson calling) amidst competing background noise.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old motorcyclist suffers from head injuries after a road traffic accident. His partner comments that his memory has become very poor. Which of the following is not a standardized test to assess his memory?
questions.explanation: The Weigl Colour–Form Sorting Test assesses executive function (categorization), not memory. AVLT, CVLT, RMT and WMT are standardized memory tests.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old male has a diagnosis of narcissistic personality disorder. He is rejected from further admission to the ward because he has made the nurses very upset by making unreasonable complaints. The nurses are begging the consultant not to admit him, although he is highly suicidal. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Countertransference refers to the emotional overreaction of staff toward a patient based on their own unconscious feelings. The nurses’ refusal reflects countertransference.

questions.question_text: All of the following are immature defence mechanisms except
questions.explanation: Humour is a mature defence mechanism. Immature defences include denial, fantasy, projection, somatization, hypochondriasis, acting out, idealization, projective identification and repression.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man is admitted to the gastroenterology ward because of abdominal pain. He has been complaining for the past 6 months that his intestines have stopped working, and said to the gastroenterologist, ‘My intestines are rotten and you can smell it.’ He has also told the doctor that he could hear his neighbours saying bad things about him. What is the most likely ICD-10 diagnosis?

options.text: Severe depressive episode with psychotic features

correct_answer.text: Severe depressive episode with psychotic features

correct_answers.text: Severe depressive episode with psychotic features

questions.explanation: Nihilistic delusions (rotting intestines) plus mood-congruent auditory hallucinations suggest a severe depressive episode with psychotic features.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements with regards to the respective delusions is incorrect?

options.text: Delusion of doubles – j’illusions de sosies

questions.explanation: Doppelgänger delusion is the false belief that a double of oneself exists. Cotard’s syndrome is a nihilistic delusion of nonexistence or organ disintegration—not a delusion of double.

questions.question_text: A gambler thinks that the more often he gambles, the more often he will win. He is not certain about the number of times gambling resulted in winning. The time interval between two episodes of winning is also unpredictable. His wife complains that he often has emotional outbursts when he pursues to win. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: A variable ratio schedule provides reinforcement (occasional wins) after an unpredictable number of responses (bets), producing high, steady response rates resistant to extinction.

questions.question_text: The following are findings from the Clinical Antipsychotic Trials of Intervention Effectiveness (CATIE) study, except

options.text: More patients taking second-generation antipsychotics continue the antipsychotic treatment compared with patients taking conventional antipsychotics.
Olanzapine was the most effective in terms of the rates of discontinuation.
The efficacy of the conventional antipsychotic agent perphenazine appeared similar to that of quetiapine, risperidone and ziprasidone.
Olanzapine was associated with greater weight gain and increases in measures of glucose and lipid metabolism.
Perphenazine was associated with more discontinuation for extrapyramidal effects.

correct_answer.text: More patients taking second-generation antipsychotics continue the antipsychotic treatment compared with patients taking conventional antipsychotics.

correct_answers.text: More patients taking second-generation antipsychotics continue the antipsychotic treatment compared with patients taking conventional antipsychotics.

questions.explanation: In CATIE more patients on conventional antipsychotic perphenazine remained on treatment compared with quetiapine, risperidone or ziprasidone. Olanzapine had the lowest discontinuation rate but greatest metabolic side-effects; perphenazine had more EPS discontinuations.

questions.question_text: A medical student reading up on the history of psychiatry found out that lactate infusion was given in the late 1960s. From his reading, the intravenous infusion of lactate caused patients to have several symptoms, which included sudden onset of palpitations, chest pain, choking sensations, dizziness, depersonalization and also a significant fear of losing control and dying. What is the psychiatric condition that has resulted from intravenous lactate infusion?
questions.explanation: Intravenous lactate infusion reliably provokes panic attacks in susceptible individuals, modelling panic disorder.

questions.question_text: A trainee wants to start a research about attitudes. He has only basic understanding that attitudes are usually based on pre-existing beliefs. Which one of the following statements associated with the measurement scale is incorrect?

options.text: Thurstone Scale – Dichotomous scale indicating agreement or disagreement
Likert Scale – More sensitive in comparison to the dichotomous Thurstone Scale
Semantic Differential Scale – Easy to use and has good test-retest reliability
Semantic Differential Scale – Positional response bias might occur

questions.explanation: The Thurstone Scale uses dichotomous agree/disagree items, but its ranking procedure can be biased and complex to implement. Likert scales are more sensitive, and semantic differential scales are bipolar visual analogue scales.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old woman has received six sessions of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). She complains of significant recent memory loss while remote memories remain intact. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: Théodule Ribot’s law states that memory dissolution is inversely related to recency: recent memories are lost while remote memories remain intact.

questions.question_text: This particular ethical principle emphasizes minimization of the risks and maximizing the benefits for the greatest number of individuals. This ethical principle is referred to as
questions.explanation: Utilitarianism focuses on outcomes that maximize overall good and minimize harm for the majority.

questions.question_text: Based on your understanding of the basic ethical principles in psychiatry, deontology refers to

options.text: Acting in the patient’s best interest.
Ensuring that the action performed is considered to be morally right if it would lead to the greatest human pleasure, happiness and satisfaction.
Ensuring that all individuals receive equal and impartial consideration.
A doctor’s motive to provide morally correct care and focus solely on the rightness and wrongness of actions, not consequences.

correct_answer.text: A doctor’s motive to provide morally correct care and focus solely on the rightness and wrongness of actions, not consequences.

correct_answers.text: A doctor’s motive to provide morally correct care and focus solely on the rightness and wrongness of actions, not consequences.

questions.explanation: Deontology emphasizes the inherent morality of actions themselves, guided by duty, regardless of outcomes.

questions.question_text: The following are ICD-10 diagnostic criteria for delusional disorder, except

options.text: There is a set of related delusions (e.g. persecutory, grandiose, hypochondriacal, jealous or erotic delusions).
The minimum duration of delusions is 6 months.
There must be no persistent hallucination.
The general criteria for schizophrenia and depressive disorder should not be fulfilled.
There must be no evidence of primary or secondary organic mental disorders.

correct_answer.text: The minimum duration of delusions is 6 months.

correct_answers.text: The minimum duration of delusions is 6 months.

questions.explanation: ICD-10 requires a minimum duration of 3 months of delusions for diagnosis, not 6 months.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man wants to transfer from another NHS trust to your trust. He is admitted to the psychiatric ward because of low mood. He complains to the ward manager that the inpatient service is not up to standard. After discharge, he has written 15 letters to the chief executive about the delay in psychologist appointment. Which of the following personality disorders is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
this man suffers from narcissistic personality disorder which is
characterised by sense of entitlement and importance.

questions.question_text: A patient was called into the interview room. Throughout the interview process, he was noted to be moving his hand repeatedly whenever he talks. This form of psychopathology is known as
questions.explanation: Mannerisms are purposive but odd and repetitive movements, often seen in psychotic disorders.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old patient with schizophrenia previously on olanzapine was diagnosed by his GP to suffer from diabetes mellitus. Her GP has written a letter to consult you on the most suitable antipsychotics to prescribe in this case. Which of the following antipsychotics would you recommend in this case?
questions.explanation: Amisulpride has minimal impact on glucose metabolism and is preferable in diabetic patients.

questions.question_text: Individuals usually tend to feel uneasy when cognitive dissonance occurs and this might lead to increased anxiety. There is always a motivation to achieve internal cognitive consistency. All of the following help with the reduction of anxiety associated with cognitive dissonance, except

options.text: Changing one or more of the thought processes involved in the dissonant relationship
Changing the behaviour that is considered inconsistent with the cognition
Addition of new thoughts that are consistent with pre-existing thought processes

questions.explanation: Cognitive dissonance is reduced by changing behaviour or cognitions or adding consonant cognitions; challenging automatic thoughts is a CBT strategy rather than a dissonance mechanism.

questions.question_text: During routine outpatient review, a patient with a diagnosis of schizophrenia, who has been concordant to his medications and has not had a relapse in the last decade, informs the psychiatrist that he wishes to stop medical treatment. The psychiatrist is concerned and cautioned him about the risk of relapse as well as the advantage and benefits of staying on the medications. The patient has mental capacity to understand and formulate a decision. However, his decision in this case would not be the best option. The psychiatrist feels compelled to go along with the wishes of the patient. This is an example of the ethical principle of
questions.explanation: Respecting the patient’s competent decision to refuse treatment illustrates the principle of autonomy.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old female teacher suffering from depression has been on sick leave for the past 6 months. She has asked the core trainee to continue giving her sick leave. The core trainee is concerned and consults you. Which of the following is an indicator for not issuing a medical certificate to this patient?

options.text: She is willing to continue the antidepressant as suggested by the core trainee.
She is keen to see a psychologist for psychotherapy as suggested by the core trainee.
She wants to be in a depressive state because her husband gives her more support when she is sick.
She is very depressed and cannot focus on teaching. She needs to be exempted from her normal social role.
She is very depressed and worries that the school will blame her for being responsible for causing her own depression.

correct_answer.text: She wants to be in a depressive state because her husband gives her more support when she is sick.

correct_answers.text: She wants to be in a depressive state because her husband gives her more support when she is sick.

questions.explanation: Seeking to remain ill for secondary gain (increased support) indicates non-medical motivation and is not a valid reason for continued sick leave.

questions.question_text: A concerned sister brought her 50-year-old brother to see you. She feels that he suffers from obsessive-compulsive personality disorder based on the information available on the Internet. Which of the following clinical features highly suggest that he indeed suffers from anankastic personality disorder?

options.text: He was asked to leave a church because he said obscene things to fellow church members.
He was fined by the traffic police for illegal parking because he tends to park anywhere on the street.
He was penalized by the HM Revenue & Customs for delay in filling up income tax form because he could not make up his mind what to report and feared making mistakes.
He was sued by his ex-wife for refusing to pay maintenance fee because he believes that she can support herself.
He was suspended from school when he was young because he vandalized school properties.

correct_answer.text: He was penalized by the HM Revenue & Customs for delay in filling up income tax form because he could not make up his mind what to report and feared making mistakes.

correct_answers.text: He was penalized by the HM Revenue & Customs for delay in filling up income tax form because he could not make up his mind what to report and feared making mistakes.

questions.explanation: Indecision and fear of making mistakes, leading to delayed tax completion, typify anankastic personality disorder.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements correctly defines what is meant by delusional perception?

options.text: It means that an abnormal perception has taken on delusional significance.
It refers to a delusional mood with delusional significance.
It means that a normal perception has taken on a delusional significance.
It means that a normal perception has been misinterpreted.
It arises due to the recall of an abnormal memory.

correct_answer.text: It means that a normal perception has taken on a delusional significance.

correct_answers.text: It means that a normal perception has taken on a delusional significance.

questions.explanation: Delusional perception is when a normal sensory experience acquires a delusional meaning for the patient.

questions.question_text: A 3-year-old boy was playing with his toy car when it rolled under the sofa. He attempted reaching for the toy car with his hands but it was too far in. After several tries at using his hands, he picked up an umbrella and succeeded at using the hook of the umbrella to reach for his toy car. Which of the following learning theories best describes the aforementioned phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Cognitive learning (insight learning) occurs when the child suddenly understands how to use the umbrella to solve the problem, without trial-and-error reinforcement.

questions.question_text: Which of the following phenomenon is the most common extrapyramidal side effect associated with the first generation antipsychotics?
questions.explanation: Akathisia (inner restlessness) occurs in up to 25% of patients on typical antipsychotics and is the most common extrapyramidal side effect.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old doctor wakes up at 6.00 am every day and goes to the hospital to ensure that the parking lot closest to the hospital main entrance is not occupied. She is easily upset with other doctors who occupy this parking lot. She could only buy fish and chips from the same store in the last 10 years and she usually declines to try other foods during lunch. She is a very clean person and likes to document in great detail. Her colleagues consult you about her personality. Your answer is
questions.explanation: Anankastic (obsessive–compulsive) personality disorder features preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism and control, as illustrated here.

questions.question_text: A 14-year-old teenager is experiencing and undergoing which stage, based on Erikson’s stage of development?
questions.explanation: Erikson’s stage of identity vs. role confusion occurs in adolescence (approximately 12–18 years).

questions.question_text: In an experiment, it was found that when there were more people around during an emergency, the participants were less likely to help. Which of the following best describes the aforementioned phenomenon?
questions.explanation: The bystander effect refers to decreased likelihood of assistance when others are present, due to diffusion of responsibility.

questions.question_text: A psychotherapist, on knowing the difficulties that his patient has experienced recently (being dismissed from work and working through the grief associated with the loss of his loved ones), mentioned to his client that ‘You have indeed coped extremely well despite the circumstances that you have been in’. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Reflective listening involves acknowledging and reflecting back the patient’s strengths and coping efforts to reinforce positive progress.

questions.question_text: A medical student was shown a list of symptoms during his psychiatry examinations and he was asked which one of the following would be helpful towards arriving at a psychiatric diagnosis for schizophrenia. What would the correct answer be?
questions.explanation: Thought withdrawal is a first-rank symptom of schizophrenia and strongly suggests the diagnosis.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man suffering from treatment-resistant schizophrenia is treated with clozapine. He wants to know the most common side effect. Your answer is
questions.explanation: Sedation is the most common side effect of clozapine, with hypersalivation being the second most common.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman with a history of depression complains of 1-week history of worsening diplopia. During physical examination, her left eye is medially deviated giving a diplopia best prevented by closing her left eye. On attempted left lateral gaze, her right eye achieves full adduction but her left eye remains static, producing a widely separated image horizontally. Which of the following conditions is most likely?
questions.explanation: Left abducens (VI) nerve palsy causes the left eye to fail to abduct, resulting in medial deviation and horizontal diplopia.

questions.question_text: A neurosurgeon was concerned about the cognitive deficits after he operated on a 23-year-old driver who had recently been involved in a traumatic road traffic accident. He referred him to the psychiatrist for further evaluation. It was found that the driver had impaired parietal lobe functioning. Which one of the following is NOT a test of parietal lobe functioning?
questions.explanation: Cognitive estimates assess frontal lobe functions (executive abilities), not parietal lobe.

questions.question_text: You are performing a risk assessment on a 20-year-old man suffering from paranoid schizophrenia. Which of the following factors is least likely to be associated with violence?

options.text: The person has access to weapons.
The person retains the ability to plan.
The person is staying in the community.
The person is totally losing touch with reality.

correct_answer.text: The person is totally losing touch with reality.

correct_answers.text: The person is totally losing touch with reality.

questions.explanation: Profound detachment from reality reduces organized, purposeful violent acts; planning and weapon access are higher risk factors.

questions.question_text: You are performing a risk assessment on a 22-year-old man suffering from acute psychosis. Which of the following conditions is least likely to be associated with violence?

options.text: He experiences hallucinations causing positive emotions.
He feels dominated by forces beyond his control.
He feels that there are people wanting to harm him.
He feels that his thoughts are being put into his head.
He reacts in despair by striking out against others.

correct_answer.text: He experiences hallucinations causing positive emotions.

correct_answers.text: He experiences hallucinations causing positive emotions.

questions.explanation: Pleasant or positive hallucinations are less likely to precipitate violence compared with threatening or control-override symptoms.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man is referred by his GP because he needs to drink one bottle of beer first thing in the morning, two bottles of beer during lunch time and at least a few glasses of hard liquor in the evening. He needs to drink to calm his nerves as he finds his job very stressful. According to his wife, he was previously diagnosed with personality disorder. Which of the following personality disorders is most likely?
questions.explanation: Anxious (avoidant) personality disorder features social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy and use of substances (e.g. alcohol) to cope with anxiety.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not considered to be a formal thought disorder?
questions.explanation:
All of the aforementioned options are considered to be part of formal
thought disorders, with the exception of (e). Asyndesis refers to the juxtaposition of
elements without adequate linkage between them. Condensation refers to combining
ideas to make the incomprehensible. Derailment refers to how the thought processes
are being derailed into a subsidiary thought. Fusion refers to how different elements
of the thought are being interwoven with each other. Other features of formal
thought disorder include omission and substitution

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old female has just been recently diagnosed with an anxiety condition known as agoraphobia. The consultant has recommended that she be started on a course of medication (antidepressants) and also a course of psychological therapy. She has been concordant thus far and has improved such that she is now able to leave home independently. Which of the following psychological interventions has helped her?
questions.explanation: Extinction occurs when the fear response diminishes after repeated exposure to the feared stimulus without avoidance or negative outcomes.

questions.question_text: A 24-year-old female patient comes for review to your outpatient clinic. The inpatient consultant prescribed olanzapine and she has taken this medication for 3 months since discharge. She complains of a weight gain of 10 kg and increased appetite. She has a family history of diabetes. She requests a change in antipsychotic. Which of the following medications would you recommend?
questions.explanation: Aripiprazole has lower metabolic side-effects and is preferred for patients concerned about weight gain and diabetes risk.

questions.question_text: A medical student new to her posting wonders at roughly what age newborns will acquire skills of accommodation and colour vision. Which of the following would be correct?
questions.explanation: Accommodation and colour vision develop around 4 months of age in infants.

questions.question_text: Psychiatry is the only specialty whose diagnoses are not confirmed by investigations but rests upon history taking. Which of the following statements regarding history taking is the most incorrect?

options.text: Assessment proforma such as admission sheets which could be found in the case notes of long-stay patients in large mental hospitals is not a good example of psychiatric history taking.
Clinical errors often occur because the clinical history itself is inadequate.
Continuing history taking is sometimes neglected because the patient is ‘well-known’ to a psychiatrist.
History taking should not be a passive process of information collection.
The standard schema of psychiatric history taking is a good guide to the structure of the psychiatric interview.

correct_answer.text: The standard schema of psychiatric history taking is a good guide to the structure of the psychiatric interview.

correct_answers.text: The standard schema of psychiatric history taking is a good guide to the structure of the psychiatric interview.

questions.explanation: A rigid standard schema can limit clinician flexibility and responsiveness; it is not always a helpful guide to the psychiatric interview.

questions.question_text: A core trainee-1 resident was interviewing an elderly man in his clinic. He decided to perform a bedside Mini Mental State Examination on the patient in view of his recent difficulties with his memory. He asked the man to copy intersecting polygons. This is a test of which part of the brain functions?
questions.explanation: Copying intersecting polygons (pentagons) assesses parietal lobe function, specifically visuoconstructional ability.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman with a history of depression complains of 1-week history of worsening diplopia. When her right eyelid is lifted, her right eye is looking down and out and the pupil is fixed and dilated. When she is asked to gaze to the left, her right eye remains in position while her left eye achieves full abduction. Which of the following conditions is most likely?
questions.explanation: Right oculomotor (III) nerve palsy causes the eye to be ‘down and out’ with ptosis and a dilated pupil.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man needs to drink alcohol immediately after he wakes up in the morning, again a few pints of beer during lunch time and again at least 8 units of alcohol in the evening. He annoys his family members who always ask him to cut down his alcohol intake. He claims that he is not an alcoholic and he needs to drink to keep himself calm. Based on the clinical information, which of the following is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Morning drinking, high tolerance and continued use despite negative consequences indicate alcohol dependence syndrome.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements with regards to delusional perception is incorrect?

options.text: Delusional perception is a primary delusion.
Delusional perception is a secondary delusion.
It might be preceded by a period of delusional mood in which the person might be aware that something strange and threatening might be happening.
It is considered to be one of the first-rank symptoms.
It usually arises fully formed without any discernible connections with prior events.

correct_answer.text: Delusional perception is a secondary delusion.

correct_answers.text: Delusional perception is a secondary delusion.

questions.explanation: Delusional perception is a primary delusion, arising fully formed without association to prior events.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old man agreed to participate in a research project. He was first given Drug A, which caused tachycardia. Five minutes later, he was given Drug B, which was supposed to cause bradycardia. Drug B was not strong enough to overcome the tachycardia associated with Drug A. The subject still had tachycardia after administration of Drug B. The administration of Drug A and Drug B was repeated 12 times over the 3 days. On the fourth day, the investigator only gave the subject Drug B and was surprised to find that he developed tachycardia. The tachycardia associated with administration of Drug B on the fourth day is known as
questions.explanation: A conditioned response is the learned tachycardia in response to Drug B alone after repeated pairing with Drug A.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man suffers from treatment-resistant schizophrenia and he is on clozapine. He also suffers from post-schizophrenia depression. Augmentation with which of the following antidepressants is the safest option in view of the potential risk of epilepsy?
questions.explanation: Fluoxetine (SSRI) has a lower risk of lowering the seizure threshold compared with bupropion or tricyclics, making it safer with clozapine.

questions.question_text: Who was responsible for discovering the use of lithium?
questions.explanation: John Cade discovered the mood-stabilizing properties of lithium in the late 1940s by demonstrating its calming effect in experimental animals and then in patients with mania.

questions.question_text: The individual who was responsible for the development of existential therapy was
questions.explanation: Viktor Frankl founded logotherapy, a form of existential therapy focusing on meaning and purpose in life.

questions.question_text: Which of the following terms best describes ‘the presence of clearly demarcated total memory loss, with no recovery of this lost memory over time’, for individuals who have experienced alcoholic blackouts?
questions.explanation: En bloc blackouts involve a continuous block of memory loss that is not recovered later, unlike fragmentary blackouts.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman develops difficulty looking down, often notable when reading or walking down stairs. Which of the following conditions is most likely?
questions.explanation: Superior oblique (IV) nerve palsy causes vertical diplopia, especially on downgaze such as reading or descending stairs.

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male who has a history of alcohol dependence was admitted just 2 days ago for an emergency hip operation following a fall. He now reports that he is troubled by visions of multiple small spiders running around the room. Which of the following correctly describes his experience?
questions.explanation: Lilliputian hallucinations involve seeing miniature figures or creatures, often seen in delirium tremens and other withdrawal states.

questions.question_text: A 39-year-old man with a history of cocaine dependence continues taking the drug to avoid experiencing withdrawal symptoms. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: Negative reinforcement occurs when a behaviour is strengthened because it removes or avoids an unpleasant state (withdrawal symptoms).

questions.question_text: A medical student wants to know the most common sign of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Your answer is
questions.explanation: Severe muscle rigidity is the hallmark and most common sign of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

questions.question_text: Based on Piaget’s theory, which stage would a child be in if he is able to recognize that containers, even though they are of different shapes, contain similar amounts of water?
questions.explanation: Conservation of volume appears in Piaget’s concrete operational stage (approx. 7–11 years).

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman with a history of depression complains of a 3-month history of worsening diplopia and ptosis in the evenings. Which of the following conditions is the most likely?
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis presents with fatigable muscle weakness, worse in the evening, causing diplopia and ptosis.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old retired naval officer with depression believes that he is in danger of imminent arrest and life imprisonment for stealing a uniform from the Royal Navy 30 years ago. The psychopathology being described is
questions.explanation: A delusion of guilt is a false belief of having done something wrong, common in severe depression.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman with a history of methamphetamine abuse reports that she continues smoking the drug because of ‘euphoria’ she experiences. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: Positive reinforcement occurs when a behaviour is strengthened by the presentation of a pleasurable stimulus (euphoria).

questions.question_text: There are reported differences in the development of boys versus girls. In particular, the average age of onset of puberty of boys is much later. Which of the following is the average age of puberty for boys?
questions.explanation: The average onset of puberty in boys is around 13 years.

questions.question_text: There are several theories that explain interpersonal attraction. Which of the following is not a theory of interpersonal attraction?
questions.explanation: Mutual attraction is a phenomenon, not a formal theory. Proxemics, social exchange, equity and reinforcement theories address interpersonal attraction.

questions.question_text: Please choose the most appropriate statements with regards to schizophrenia:

options.text: Afro-Caribbean immigrants to the United Kingdom have a much lower risk of developing schizophrenia.
The winter excess of births in schizophrenics is due to a seasonal prevalence of a viral infection or other perinatal hazard.
Males have generally a later onset of schizophrenia as compared to females.
It has been found that there is a reduction in the relapse rates of schizophrenia in those who have lived with families in which the relatives displayed high EE.
Obstetric complications are less likely in individuals with schizophrenia.

correct_answer.text: The winter excess of births in schizophrenics is due to a seasonal prevalence of a viral infection or other perinatal hazard.

correct_answers.text: The winter excess of births in schizophrenics is due to a seasonal prevalence of a viral infection or other perinatal hazard.

questions.explanation: Only the winter excess of births is attributed to seasonal perinatal infections. The other statements are false.

questions.question_text: A mother worries that her daughter will develop depression because of the family history of depressive disorder. Which of the following genes is associated with increased risk?
questions.explanation: The serotonin transporter gene (5-HTTLPR) has been linked to increased susceptibility to depressive disorders.

questions.question_text: During a clinical examination, a core trainee was asked what terminology would best describe ‘memories for events occurring while intoxicated are lost when sober, but return when next intoxicated’. Which of the following would be the most appropriate terminology?
questions.explanation: State-dependent memory refers to retrieval of information being tied to the physiological or psychological state present at encoding.

questions.question_text: A 22-year-old male, Jack, is usually not an aggressive person. However, in 2011, while participating in a large-scale riot in London that turned violent, Jack found himself engaged in violence as well. Which of the following best explains Jack’s behaviour?
questions.explanation: Deindividuation occurs in large groups when individuals lose self-awareness and restraints, leading to behaviour inconsistent with their usual selves.

questions.question_text: At what age does a British child start to have early comprehension of English grammar?
questions.explanation: Between ages 3 and 6, children develop rudimentary grammar and sentence structures as part of the preschool language explosion.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man presents with unequal pupils, right-sided ptosis and anhidrosis of the right half of the face and body. The patient is most likely suffering from?
questions.explanation: The triad of miosis, ptosis and facial anhidrosis indicates Horner’s syndrome due to sympathetic pathway disruption.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old man meets the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia and exhibits passivity phenomena. Passivity phenomena include the following, except
questions.explanation: Passivity phenomena involve insertion, withdrawal or broadcasting of thoughts and made feelings/impulses; thought blocking is a thought disorder, not a passivity phenomenon.

questions.question_text: A 14-year-old girl was disallowed to meet her friends over the weekend as she was caught lying to her parents. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: Punishment is the application of an unpleasant consequence (withholding weekend privileges) to decrease unwanted behaviour (lying).

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man has been prescribed with lithium, haloperidol and fluoxetine. A trainee consults you because the patient has developed a tremor. Which of the following features suggest that the tremor is caused by haloperidol?
questions.explanation: Haloperidol can induce parkinsonism, characterised by a coarse 'pill-rolling' tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia rather than a fine lithium-like tremor.

questions.question_text: Attention refers to an intensive process in which information selection takes place. Which one of the following statements is true?

options.text: Dichotic listening studies test for selective attention.
With divided attention, performance is enhanced.
Attention is the equivalent of working memory.
Attention involves information retrieval from the short-term memory storage.
Attention involves information retrieval from the long-term memory storage.

correct_answer.text: Dichotic listening studies test for selective attention.

correct_answers.text: Dichotic listening studies test for selective attention.

questions.explanation: Dichotic listening paradigms require subjects to attend selectively to one auditory channel while ignoring another, illustrating selective attention.

questions.question_text: You are the trainee psychiatrist in the child and adolescent mental health service (CAMHS). An anxious mother brings her 2-year-old daughter for developmental assessment. She is concerned about her daughter’s language and speech development. Which of the following developmental milestones is expected of her daughter?
questions.explanation: Telegraphic speech (short two- to three-word phrases) typically emerges by 24 months.

questions.question_text: Autochthonous delusions are
questions.explanation: Autochthonous (primary) delusions are ego-syntonic, experienced as self-generated and in harmony with the self.

questions.question_text: The case of Phineas Gage describes which of the following syndrome?
questions.explanation: Phineas Gage’s injury to the frontal lobes led to personality and executive function changes, exemplifying frontal lobe syndrome.

questions.question_text: Which of the following will predispose the child to emotional problems later in life?

options.text: Transitional object for more than 6 months in the first year of life
Upbringing in an authoritarian family setting

correct_answer.text: Upbringing in an authoritarian family setting

correct_answers.text: Upbringing in an authoritarian family setting

questions.explanation: Authoritarian parenting (high control, low warmth) is linked to later emotional and behavioural problems.

questions.question_text: A core trainee presents a list of symptoms for neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). The following are symptoms of NMS, except?

options.text: NMS presents within 48 hours after the initiation of a new antipsychotic

correct_answer.text: NMS presents within 48 hours after the initiation of a new antipsychotic

correct_answers.text: NMS presents within 48 hours after the initiation of a new antipsychotic

questions.explanation: NMS can occur at any time during antipsychotic treatment, not specifically within the first 48 hours.

questions.question_text: A drug company wants to promote its new antidepressants. Patients will get one box of antidepressants free of charge if they purchase three boxes of antidepressants at one time. This phenomenon is known as
questions.explanation: A fixed-ratio schedule provides reinforcement (free box) after a set number of responses (purchase of three boxes).

questions.question_text: Morbid jealousy is not

options.text: More common in men than in women

questions.explanation: Morbid jealousy (Othello syndrome) is a delusional disorder of infidelity, not a misidentification syndrome (e.g. Capgras, Fregoli).

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man has had a stroke recently. He is concerned about developing dementia and wants to find out which medication could prevent vascular dementia. The correct answer is
questions.explanation: Antiplatelet therapy (low-dose aspirin) can reduce recurrent infarcts and may help prevent vascular dementia.

questions.question_text: Previous research has found which of the following to be an important protective factor for Alzheimer’s dementia?
questions.explanation: Cognitive reserve from higher education is associated with lower risk and later onset of Alzheimer’s dementia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a primary prevention strategy in children and adolescents?

options.text: Easing the impact of traumatic milestones and transitional events in school and family
Preventing vulnerable population from succumbing to psychiatric disorder
Preventing the onset of carefully defined psychiatric disorder
Promoting and enhancing adaptability and healthy functioning
Measuring intelligence at regular intervals from children to adolescence

correct_answer.text: Measuring intelligence at regular intervals from children to adolescence

correct_answers.text: Measuring intelligence at regular intervals from children to adolescence

questions.explanation: Regular IQ testing is assessment, not a primary prevention strategy, which focuses on reducing risk factors and strengthening resilience.

questions.question_text: In this particular type of attention, at least two sources of information are attended to simultaneously and the performance is inefficient.
questions.explanation: Divided attention requires processing multiple inputs at once, leading to decreased efficiency (dual-task interference).

questions.question_text: This particular type of attention is commonly described as the cocktail party effect.
questions.explanation: Selective or focused attention allows one to tune into a single stimulus (your name) while filtering out others.

questions.question_text: In this particular type of attention, the environment is monitored over a long period of time.
questions.explanation: Sustained attention or vigilance involves prolonged monitoring, with performance often declining over time.

questions.question_text: In this particular type of attention, the subject becomes so skilled with the task that little conscious effort is now required.
questions.explanation: Automatic attention requires minimal conscious effort once a skill is well practiced.

questions.question_text: This is a memory test that could be utilized in clinical settings to estimate the premorbid intelligence quotient.
questions.explanation: The National Adult Reading Test (NART) uses irregular word-reading to estimate premorbid IQ, as vocabulary is relatively preserved.

questions.question_text: This is a test that tests for the perception of relations between abstract items.
questions.explanation: Raven’s Progressive Matrices assess non-verbal abstract reasoning by identifying patterns in visual matrices.

questions.question_text: This is a memory test battery that has an emphasis on tests related to skills required in daily living.
questions.explanation: The Rivermead Behavioural Memory Test focuses on everyday memory tasks (route recall, story, faces) relevant to daily functioning.

questions.question_text: This particular test is effective in testing for brain damage as well as early cognitive decline.
questions.explanation: The Benton Visual Retention Test evaluates visual memory and immediate recall, sensitive to brain injury and early cognitive impairment.

questions.question_text: Non-dominant temporal lobe damage can lead potentially to impaired performance on this test, whereas dominant temporal lobe damage tends not to.
questions.explanation: The Rey–Osterrieth Complex Figure Test is more impaired by right (non-dominant) temporal–parietal lesions affecting visuospatial memory.

questions.question_text: This is the dogmatic belief that one race is superior to another one and that there exist identifiable racial characteristics which influence cognition, achievement and behaviour.
questions.explanation: Prejudice is a preconceived negative attitude toward a group, often based on stereotypes about race or other characteristics.

questions.question_text: This terminology refers to the enactment of prejudice.
questions.explanation: Discrimination is the behavioural manifestation or enactment of prejudiced attitudes.

questions.question_text: This terminology refers to the experience of discrimination of an individual who bears a stigma.
questions.explanation: Enacted stigma refers to actual experiences of prejudice or discrimination by the stigmatized individual.

questions.question_text: This terminology refers to the fear of discrimination of an individual who bears a stigma.
questions.explanation: Felt stigma is the anticipation or fear of being discriminated against by others.

questions.question_text: This is the operating system of the preconscious and the conscious.
questions.explanation: Secondary process thinking, governed by reality testing, operates in the preconscious and conscious mind.

questions.question_text: This is deemed to be the operating system of the unconscious.
questions.explanation: Primary process thinking, driven by the pleasure principle, operates in the unconscious.

questions.question_text: This contains memories, ideas and affects that are typically repressed.
questions.explanation: The unconscious mind holds repressed content inaccessible to conscious awareness.

questions.question_text: This is the part of the mind that develops during childhood and serves to maintain repression and censorship.
questions.explanation:
characteristic features of preconscious are that it is outside
awareness and the operating system is secondary process thinking. the access can
occur through focused attention

questions.question_text: Based on the structural model of the mind, this is considered to be unconscious. It contains primordial energy reserves derived from instinctual drives.
questions.explanation: The id is entirely unconscious and houses instinctual drives, operating on the pleasure principle.

questions.question_text: Based on the structural model of the mind, this helps to fulfill the task of self-preservation.
questions.explanation: The ego mediates between impulse and reality, enabling self-preservation and adaptive functioning.

questions.question_text: Antipsychotics are usually not indicated for mild-to-moderate non-cognitive symptoms because of the risk of severe adverse events.
questions.explanation: Patients with dementia with Lewy bodies are highly sensitive to neuroleptics and at risk for severe reactions.

questions.question_text: Patients with this form of dementia tend to have a younger age of onset, with more severe apathy, disinhibition, reduction in speech output, loss of insight and coarsening of social behaviour.
questions.explanation: Frontotemporal dementia presents earlier and features behavioural changes such as disinhibition and apathy.

questions.question_text: This form of dementia is characterized by a stepwise deteriorating course with a patchy distribution of neurological and neuropsychological deficits.
questions.explanation: Vascular dementia often shows a stepwise decline corresponding to successive infarcts.

questions.question_text: In this form of dementia, on CT scan, there is noted to be progressive subcortical vascular encephalopathy with CT scan revealing markedly enlarged ventricles secondary to infarction in hemispheric white matter.
questions.explanation: Binswanger’s disease (subcortical leukoencephalopathy) shows white matter infarcts and ventricular enlargement.

questions.question_text: This is a form of dementia that is more common in males.
questions.explanation:
An excess of vascular dementia has been noted in males, which is likely
to be due to the increased prevalence of cardiovascular disease in men.

questions.question_text: This is a condition in which the patient intentionally produces physical or psychological symptoms and the patient is fully aware of his or her underlying motives.
questions.explanation: Malingering involves deliberate symptom fabrication for external gain, with conscious awareness of motives.

questions.question_text: In this condition, the patient intentionally produces physical and psychological symptoms but the patient is unconscious about his or her underlying motives.
questions.explanation: Factitious disorder features deliberate symptom production but with unconscious motivation—seek the sick role.

questions.question_text: Patients with this condition usually present with persistent, severe, distressing pain, which cannot be explained by physical disorder.
questions.explanation: Persistent somatoform pain disorder involves chronic, medically unexplained pain causing significant distress and impairment.

questions.question_text: This occurs usually on the third to the fifth day after pregnancy and occurs in about 50% of women.
questions.explanation: Postnatal blues begins 2–5 days postpartum, with tearfulness, mood lability and mild anxiety in up to 50% of new mothers.

questions.question_text: Poor social adjustment, marital relationship and fear of labour are predisposing factors leading to the development of this condition.
questions.explanation: Risk factors for postnatal blues include poor social support, marital discord and apprehension about childbirth.

questions.question_text: This condition has an abrupt onset, usually within the first 2 weeks after childbirth, and there might be rapid changes in mental state, sometimes from hour to hour.
questions.explanation: Puerperal psychosis typically has sudden onset within 2 weeks postpartum with rapidly fluctuating mood, delusions and hallucinations.

questions.question_text: This condition occurs in 10%–15% of postpartum women usually within 3 months of childbirth.
questions.explanation: Postnatal depression affects about 10–15% of new mothers, usually emerging within the first three months after delivery.

questions.question_text: This is a condition that has a higher prevalence in those around the age of 30 years, and the prevalence increases with increasing parity.
questions.explanation: Premenstrual syndrome prevalence peaks in the late twenties to early thirties and may be influenced by number of pregnancies (parity).

questions.question_text: This is one of the best-known psychiatrists during the Victorian era. He was the first person to propose the abolishment of physical restraints in England.
questions.explanation: He was the first person to propose the abolishment of physical restraints in England. He went on to become one of the best known psychiatrists. He believed psychiatric illness to be a physical disorder of the body, much similar to other medical illnesses.

questions.question_text: He was first to develop the technique of psychoanalysis.
questions.explanation: He initially started studying cases of hysteria using hypnosis. Then he began to develop the technique of psychoanalysis, which was later used to explain the psychological causes of symptoms.

questions.question_text: This led to the formation of the terminology ‘Soldier’s heart’ during the American Civil War.
questions.explanation: He coined the term Da Costa’s syndrome or Soldier’s heart during the American Civil War. This condition is a functional heart disease and the soldiers presented with left-sided chest pain, palpitation, breathlessness, sweating and fatigue during exertion.

questions.question_text: Broca’s aphasia was coined by which one of the aforementioned individuals?
questions.explanation: Paul Broca coined the terminology Broca’s aphasia, which involves a lesion in the ventro-posterior region of the frontal lobe. This leads to Broca’s aphasia that affects speech production but not comprehension.

questions.question_text: This individual proposed the degeneration theory that states that mental illness affecting one generation can be passed on to the next generation in ever-worsening degrees.
questions.explanation: He proposed the degeneration theory that states that mental illness affecting one generation can be passed on to the next generation in ever-worsening degrees.

questions.question_text: This code emphasizes that all experiments should avoid suffering and injury.
questions.explanation: The Nuremberg code was developed in wartime tribunal against the Nazi German doctors. The main objective is to protect human rights during experiments and research. An experiment should avoid suffering and injury.

questions.question_text: This code emphasizes that seeking consent from research subjects is absolutely necessary.
questions.explanation: It is stated in the Nuremberg code that proper preparations should be performed to protect research subjects and the experiments should be conducted by qualified personnel. Subjects have the liberty to withdraw at any time, and investigators must stop if continuation risks injury or death.

questions.question_text: This code states the importance of formulation in research protocol and informs the subjects of the protocol details.
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Helsinki states that the principal investigator must balance predictable risks and foreseeable benefits, respect integrity and privacy, obtain consent freely, and preserve accuracy in publication of results.

questions.question_text: This code emphasizes on the importance of justice.
questions.explanation: The Belmont report emphasizes justice: ensuring research benefits are distributed fairly, with equal and impartial consideration of subjects.

questions.question_text: These patients tend to have marked emotional coldness and have little interest in activities that provide pleasure or in relationships.
questions.explanation: Individuals with schizoid personality disorder tend to have a solitary lifestyle, are indifferent to praise and criticism, and have no interest in relationships or sexual experiences. They have few friends and are cold and detached.

questions.question_text: These patients tend to have unusual perceptions, are friendless and have odd beliefs and speech. They might also have ideas of reference.
questions.explanation: Patients with schizotypal personality disorder tend to have unusual perceptions, odd beliefs and speech, ideas of reference, inappropriate or constricted affect, and few friends outside first-degree relatives.

questions.question_text: These are individuals who bear grudges without justification and are excessively sensitive to attacks.
questions.explanation: Patients with paranoid personality disorder tend to bear grudges without justification, are excessively sensitive, and often interpret benign remarks as threatening or demeaning.
